Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.question: Besides Mary, John, Rebecca, William and Joseph, who were the other children of Thomas Hale (b. about 1810, Pennsylvania; d. 1868, Greene County, Ohio) and his wife Sarah?
items.rationale: Primary research objective. The tree holds the couple and five children; no records have been searched yet for any others.

planItems.rationale: The 1850 census is the first federal schedule that names every household member. The tree holds Thomas Hale (about 1810, Pennsylvania) and Sarah with children Mary (about 1836), John (about 1838), Rebecca (about 1841), William (about 1844) and Joseph (about 1847), all born in Greene County per the tree. Search the United States Census, 1850 collection (name-searchable) for the Thomas Hale household and read every listed child, including any older child at home or a child living in a neighboring household. Any child in the household not already in the tree is a direct answer to the question.

Ten years on, children still at home and any late-born child under about 13 appear by name with relationship to the household. Search the United States Census, 1860 collection (name-searchable) for Thomas and Sarah Hale and compare the household against the 1850 list. A child absent in 1860 may have married or died; that absence is a lead, not a conclusion.

The tree records Thomas's death in 1868, so the 1870 household should be headed by Sarah, a widow, if she was still living in Greene County. Search the United States Census, 1870 collection (name-searchable) for Sarah Hale and for any Hale household with a widow at its head, and list every child at home. Any unlisted child is a lead.

The 1880 census gives each person's relationship to the head of household, which separates children from in-laws and grandchildren. Search the United States Census, 1880 collection (name-searchable) for Sarah Hale living with a son or daughter, and for the adult Hale children in their own households, so that any child not yet in the tree can be matched by name, age and birthplace.
The 1840 census in the United States Census, 1840 collection (name-searchable) names only the head of household and tallies other members by age bracket, so it cannot name any child.
planItems.skip_reason: The 1840 schedule names only the head; the 1850 census (sequence 1) is the first that names each child, so 1840 cannot answer which children the couple had.

planItems.rationale: The couple's marriage predates Mary's birth of about 1836 and probably falls in the 1825-1836 window. Search Ohio, County Marriages, 1789-2016 (name-searchable) for Thomas Hale and Sarah. The marriage dates the start of the family and may name Sarah's parents, but it supplies her maiden name only if this was her first marriage; treat any surname it gives her as provisional until a second marriage is ruled out. The marriage could have taken place in Pennsylvania instead, which this item does not cover.

Ohio civil birth registration in the county is thin before the late 1860s, so christenings are the route to children born before Mary (about 1836) and to any child born after 1847. Search Ohio, Church and Civil Births and Baptisms, 1765-1947 and Ohio, Church Records, 1762-2008 (both name-searchable) for Hale entries naming Thomas and Sarah as parents. Also check Ohio, County Births, 1841-2003 (name-searchable) for any civil birth entry naming the couple. A child baptised elsewhere would not appear here, which is why sequence 6 and the Pennsylvania side remain open.

The tree records Thomas Hale's death in Greene County in 1868. His death or burial entry may name surviving children, or Sarah as widow, and a burial record can place family graves together. Search Ohio, Deaths and Burials, 1854-1997 and Ohio, County Death Records, 1840-2001 (both name-searchable) for Thomas Hale in 1868, reading any informant or survivor line.

Thomas's estate after his death in 1868 was handled by the Greene County Probate Court (the Court of Common Pleas held probate until 1852, per the locality entry). Ohio, Probate Records, 1789-1996 is browse-only, so this is an image browse of the 1868 estate or guardianship files for Hale, which often list heirs by name. The end date is set by Sarah's plausible lifespan (she was likely born about 1815 and so could have died by about 1890), not by the 1868 death alone, so a later estate or guardianship for her still falls inside the window.

The tree holds no death date for Sarah Hale. Her death record, if found, may name her parents and her children, and Sarah's death may fall after the 1880 census. Search Ohio, County Death Records, 1840-2001 and Ohio, Deaths and Burials, 1854-1997 (both name-searchable) for Sarah Hale in Greene County, reading any parent or survivor line. The window ends at about 1900, which is past the age a woman born about 1815 would reach by the 1880s.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

planItems.rationale: Parents' marriage. Thomas Flynn (b. ~1818 per the 1850 and 1860 censuses) must have married before Patrick's birth (~1845). Pennsylvania Church Marriages, 1682-1976 is name-searchable. The entry gives the mother's maiden name only if it was her first marriage, so item 2 tests for remarriage. It confirms the couple as a unit, not that Patrick is their child. Catholic registers are held by the parish and the Diocese of Philadelphia, not the county, so any indexed hit must be checked against the register image.

Fallback for item 1: Pennsylvania County Marriages, 1775-1991 is name-searchable. The window runs past the parents' marriage to catch any later marriage of Thomas's wife, since a surname in one marriage record may be a prior married name. Each of her marriage records is searched as its own entry, so no maiden name is taken from a single record. Bondsmen and witnesses named here are FAN leads.

Patrick's baptism, which names his parents. Pennsylvania Births and Christenings, 1709-1950 is name-searchable. The 1850 and 1860 censuses give his birthplace as Ireland, so a Pennsylvania baptism is unlikely unless the family arrived before he was baptized. Search Thomas Flynn as father; a hit in a Schuylkill parish register would be the first record placing Patrick with Thomas by name.

Thomas Flynn's will or administration, filed with the Schuylkill County Register of Wills (records from 1811). Thomas was last known alive in 1860 (1860 census). A will naming Patrick as a son is direct parentage evidence. The FamilySearch collection Pennsylvania Probate Records, 1683-1994 is browse-only, so this is an image browse of the county dockets, not a name search. The window runs to 1900 because a file can be filed years after death.
Fallback for item 4: a direct request to the Schuylkill County Register of Wills for Thomas Flynn's estate file, if the browse-only images do not show it. Same window and purpose as item 4.

Thomas Flynn's death or burial. Pennsylvania Deaths and Burials, 1720-1999 and Pennsylvania Cemetery Records, ca. 1700-ca. 1950 are name-searchable. A death entry usually states an age or birthplace, which can confirm Thomas's birth around 1818 and the place where he died, and it fixes the death year that sizes item 4.

Mortality schedule for Schuylkill County, which lists deaths in a census year. The United States Census (Mortality Schedule), 1850-1880 collection is name-searchable. If Thomas died in 1860, 1870 or 1880 this names him with his age and place of death, which fixes the death year for item 4.

Patrick Flynn's own estate file (he died 12 March 1908). Heirs and their relationship to him may be named there, and an estate file could list a brother or sibling who shares Thomas as father. The Pennsylvania Probate Records, 1683-1994 collection is browse-only. The window runs to 1915 because administration can run past the death.

FAN item: baptisms of Patrick's siblings, which name the same parents. Pennsylvania Births and Christenings, 1709-1950 is name-searchable; search Flynn with Thomas as father and the mother's given name once item 1 supplies it. A sibling's record that names Thomas and the mother places Patrick in the same family without relying on the census household alone.

8. The 1850–1880 mortality schedules, for Thomas's death.
9. A delayed birth registration for Patrick, testing the Pennsylvania birthplace.
10. Thomas's naturalization, if he took papers in Pennsylvania.

**Two gaps:**
- Patrick's birthplace conflicts between Ireland (census) and Pennsylvania (death certificate). The locality entry covers Pennsylvania only, so no Irish baptism or civil-record item is planned. An Irish locality survey is needed before one can be.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1775-1991 and Pennsylvania, Church Marriages, 1682-1976 are both name-searchable per loc_001. This marriage supplies the mother's maiden name if it was her first marriage, and by its date before the 1845 birth it corroborates Thomas as father; it does not by itself prove Patrick is their child. Search the surname Flynn as groom, then the wife's given name once found.

FAN-directed: baptisms of Flynn children whose entries name Thomas Flynn as father and his wife as mother. Pennsylvania, Births and Christenings, 1709-1950 is name-searchable per loc_001. Sibling baptisms name both parents directly, which is the parentage evidence the census households lack. Search the surname Flynn with father Thomas, across both parish and county entries; the Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia, so search by county, not by diocese.

FAN-directed: the 1908 death certificate's informant was son-in-law James Brown, so he married a Flynn daughter, a sister of Patrick. Her marriage record names Thomas Flynn as her father, which is a sibling's record naming the same parents. Search Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1775-1991 (name-searchable) for a James Brown groom marrying a Flynn bride in Schuylkill County, and Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677-1950 (name-searchable) as the alternate.

FAN-directed: neighbours of the Thomas Flynn household (dwelling 84, per pli_001's log) in the 1850 census. Pennsylvania families of Irish birth lived in clusters, and a neighbour or boarder with a shared surname or the same Irish birthplace can name Thomas's wife or the household's kin. The 1850 census is a name-searchable national collection (United States, Census, 1850). The household's relationships are inferred, not stated, so this item reads the household and its adjacent dwellings for who lived with Thomas and whether a Flynn kin appears next door.

Thomas Flynn's estate, if he died in this window: a will or administration naming his children, including Patrick, would be direct parentage evidence. The window runs from the child's 1845 birth to about 1900, sized to Thomas's lifespan (b. ~1818, so he would be about 82 by 1900), not the subject's research window. Pennsylvania, Wills and Deeds, ca. 1700s-2017 is name-searchable per loc_001. Search Thomas Flynn as decedent and his wife as administrator or widow.

Fallback for the estate search above: the Schuylkill Register of Wills probate dockets, which the locality entry places from 1811, are a browse-only image group (Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994). Browse the dockets image by image for Flynn estates in the window if the name search returns nothing. Estates of Irish-born men were often filed without the decedent's birthplace, so browse by the year of death rather than by place of birth.

The subject's own burial entry, since he died 12 March 1908 and the death certificate's informant was an in-law: a burial register or cemetery record can name the parents' home parish or give the family plot, where Thomas Flynn may also be buried. Search Patrick Flynn with death year 1908 in Schuylkill County, then search Thomas Flynn in the same cemetery for the family plot.

Thomas Flynn's own death: the mortality schedules of the 1850-1880 censuses list those who died in the year before each census, with age and birthplace. If Thomas died in that window, the entry fixes the date and place of his death, which bears on where the estate was filed. United States Census (Mortality Schedule), 1850-1880 is name-searchable, and Pennsylvania, Mortality Schedules, 1850-1880 is name-searchable per loc_001.

Patrick's birth in Pennsylvania: the death certificate's informant gave Pennsylvania as birthplace, while the census households say Ireland. A delayed birth registration filed in Pennsylvania would test the claim and name the parents if one exists. Pennsylvania, Delayed Birth Records, 1780-1977 is name-searchable per loc_001. A delayed-registration record that names Thomas would be a direct parentage source; its absence neither confirms nor rules out Irish birth.

Thomas Flynn's naturalization, if he took out papers in Pennsylvania: a declaration or petition often names the wife and minor children, and a naturalized Irish-born man's family is the parentage link. Pennsylvania, Eastern District Court, Naturalization Records, 1795-1952 and Pennsylvania, Middle District Court, Naturalization Records, 1901-1992 are both name-searchable per loc_001; the court district for Schuylkill County is to be confirmed before the search. Search Thomas Flynn with birth year about 1818 and Ireland as birthplace.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1870-1882

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1870-1882

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) -- browse image-by-image.

# Utah research guide (Weber County)

## Online records
- **U.S. federal censuses, 1940 and 1950** - indexed on FamilySearch; list each household member with relationship to the head.
- **Utah land and property records** - county recorder deeds; index online for some counties. Name grantors and grantees only.

items.notes: 1940 U.S. Census, South Boise Election Precinct, Ada County, Idaho — household of John O. and Olive Applegarth with son Alan (age 4).
1950 U.S. Census, Ogden, Weber County, Utah — household of John O and Olive H Applegarth with Alan. Corroborates the 1940 household.
Marriage of John Obrien Applegarth and Olive Annie Harvey, 20 Oct 1926, Weber County, Utah. Establishes the parental couple and the mother's maiden name (Harvey).
2023 obituary for Alan Glen Applegarth (GenealogyBank) names his parents (preceded in death by John O. and Olive Harvey Applegarth). Independent corroboration of the parentage.
No christening or LDS baptism record located for Alan; the family does not appear in the searched parish/LDS registers.
No probate located for either parent (Olive d. 1970, John d. 1998) that enumerates children.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

planItems.rationale: Patrick Flynn's death fact (F2, 1908-03-12, Schuylkill County) is sourced to S3, Pennsylvania Death Certificates, but the tree records no parent names from it. Statewide certificates from 1906 usually name the decedent's father and mother, which is direct parentage evidence. Pull the certificate itself, not only the index entry, and read the parents' names and birthplaces. Pennsylvania, Deaths and Burials, 1720-1999 is name-searchable and can locate the entry; the certificate image may need a request, so access is unknown.

The 1860 United States census is name-searchable and is in the tree as S2 but has no search logged. The 1850 entry (dwelling 84, Thomas Flynn's household) is the only household found so far. Find Patrick, age about 15, under Thomas Flynn and record his relationship to the head, birthplace (the 1850 entry says Ireland while the objective says Pennsylvania, so this test is needed), and every other household member. Also search the household for a mother and siblings.

The 1880 census is the first to give each person's relationship to the head of household, and it gives parents' birthplaces. If Patrick is living with a father or a widowed mother, 1880 can confirm the child link directly. Search for Patrick by birth range re-derived from each census age, with birthplace Ireland or Pennsylvania, and search every household member.

The 1870 census lies between the 1860 and 1880 enumerations and may show Thomas Flynn's household, a widowed mother, or a change in composition. Search for Thomas Flynn and Patrick Flynn with the birth range from the other censuses, and search each household member.

Patrick died in 1908, so the census years after 1850 up to his death run through 1900 (1890 is skipped). The 1900 census also records the year and birthplace of each marriage, which bears on the parents' marriage date. Search for Patrick and every household member, keyed on his birth range and birthplace Ireland or Pennsylvania.

FAN item. The log shows that Patrick's 1850 entry sits in dwelling 84 with Thomas Flynn. Browse the 1850 neighbours of dwelling 84 for other Flynn households and for Irish-born families with the same surname. A relative such as a brother of Thomas, or a mother's family, may be the household that shows the parentage. The only parentage evidence available here is co-residence, which is indirect.

Parents' marriage item. Search Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1775-1991 (name-searchable) for Thomas Flynn, about born 1818, marrying before 1846. This marriage gives the mother's maiden name only if it was her first marriage, so record every marriage of Thomas found and the surname each one gives the wife. Pair with the parish marriage register item below. The marriage proves the union but does not by itself show that Patrick is their child.

Schuylkill County stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia until 1961, and Catholic marriage registers are held at the parish or diocese, not the county. The county marriage index may miss a parish-only marriage. Plan a visit or request to the parish register that covers Schuylkill Catholic families, for Thomas Flynn's marriage, with the mother's name and parents' names. Access is unknown; the item is inactive until a parish is identified.

Pennsylvania, Births and Christenings, 1709-1950 is name-searchable. Search for a baptism of Patrick Flynn about 1845 that names Thomas Flynn and a mother as parents, which would test both the parentage and the birthplace conflict (Ireland in the tree, Pennsylvania in the objective). Also search for baptisms of siblings of Patrick with Thomas Flynn as father, 1840-1865. Sibling baptisms name the same parents and are direct evidence of the family unit.

Probate is the primary parentage source for the county. Schuylkill County Register of Wills holds wills and administrations from 1811. Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994 is browse-only, so this is an image browse of the Flynn entries, not a name search. Look for an estate of Thomas Flynn naming Patrick as a son, and for Patrick's own 1908 estate naming his heirs and mother. The window runs to 1910 because a parent of a child born about 1845 could die well after the child's birth.

If Thomas Flynn died while Patrick was a minor, the orphans' court would have a guardianship or estate docket naming the minor children and the widow. The locality entry shows the court's marriage and adoption records from 1885, but it does not date its estate dockets, so access and coverage are unknown. This item is a fallback to the probate item above if the Register of Wills has no entry.

Pennsylvania, Cemetery Records, ca. 1700-ca. 1950 is name-searchable. Search for Thomas Flynn and Patrick Flynn in Schuylkill County burial records. A family plot may list the wife and children with death dates, which names members of the household without a surname search on the census.

Patrick died in 1908, and a Catholic burial entry at his parish can name his parents, his age and his birthplace. The sacramental registers are held at the parish or the diocese, not the county, and access is unknown. This item covers the subject's own burial entry and tests the parentage and the birthplace conflict. It is the fallback if the death certificate or cemetery record does not name the parents.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

items.question: Who were the parents of Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845, PA, d. 1908)?
items.rationale: This is the primary research objective.

planItems.rationale: The 1880 census is the first enumeration that states each person's relationship to the head of household, so it can directly test whether Patrick Flynn (about 35) is Thomas Flynn's son. The 1850 and 1860 placements (log_001, log_004) are indirect because those censuses name no relationships. Searched as a name-searchable national collection. Patrick's birthplace is not used as a search key because it is disputed (Ireland in the censuses, Pennsylvania on the death certificate, conflict c_001). Thomas Flynn (born about 1818) should be the head or a near-head in the household.

Tests continued co-residence of Patrick (about 25) with Thomas Flynn (about 52) after the 1850 and 1860 placements (log_001, log_004). It is a name-searchable national census. Search by a birth range around 1845 and by Irish birthplace, plus the surname, and then search every household member; do not key on the disputed Pennsylvania birthplace. The 1870 census names no relationships, so this is indirect evidence, and the item is also needed to close the gap noted in ps_001.

The 1900 census is required by the disputed-fact rule (birth about 1845, death 1908, so the census years after 1850 are 1860, 1870, 1880 and 1900; 1890 is largely lost). It names relationships to the head, and Patrick would be about 55. Search by the Irish birth range and the surname, and check any household headed by a Thomas Flynn born about 1818 whose household includes Patrick or a Patrick Flynn born about 1845. Name-searchable national collection.

The parents' marriage: Thomas Flynn married before Patrick's birth (about 1845). The marriage supplies the mother's maiden name if this was her first marriage, and by its date it corroborates Thomas as father, but it does not by itself prove Patrick is their child (see the census and probate items for that). Search Thomas Flynn in the name-searchable county marriage collection, and also in the civil marriage collection, since the record may sit in either. The mother's identity is unknown, so search by Thomas's name and not by a guessed bride's name.

Thomas Flynn's will or administration, held by the county Register of Wills (quirk in loc_001). A will naming Patrick as a son would be direct parentage evidence and is the strongest test ps_001 says is still missing. The window is sized to Thomas's possible lifespan (born about 1818, so a death from about 1845 to about 1905), not to the subject's window. The probate collection is browse-only, so this is an image browse of the Schuylkill dockets, not a name search.

FAN item. The 1850 census dwellings adjacent to dwelling 84 (Thomas Flynn's household, log_001) hold other Irish-born families. Search for Flynn households and Irish-born households within a few dwellings of 84, to find a sibling, a cousin or a boarder who may be a relative. If a Flynn child of about the right age appears there, it would bear on whether Patrick belongs to Thomas's family line. This is a name-searchable national census, and it tests the subject's family from outside the subject's own record.

Remarriage check for Thomas Flynn. If Thomas married again after the first marriage, the first marriage record may not name Patrick's mother. ps_001 and the parents' marriage item rely on a single marriage record, so any later Thomas Flynn marriage in the county must be found before the mother's maiden name can be treated as settled. Search by the groom's name in the name-searchable county marriage collection.

Patrick Flynn's burial, after his death of 12 March 1908 recorded in his death certificate (log_005). A burial record or a family plot in a Schuylkill County cemetery may place Thomas Flynn or a wife in the same plot, which would be indirect corroboration. The cemetery collection is name-searchable, but burial registers seldom name parents, so this is a corroborating item, not a parentage item on its own.

The subject's own birth or baptism: the birth is recorded as Ireland in the 1850 and 1860 censuses. Civil birth registration in Ireland began only in 1864, so no civil birth certificate can exist for a birth about 1845. The only route is a parish baptism, which is not reachable until the county and parish are known.

The marriage gives the date that places the first child and confirms the couple as a unit. It also shows whether the marriage was her first, which matters because she married Martin Kearney in 1879 (log_001). Also search Pennsylvania Church Marriages (1682-1976), which is name-searchable, for a parish record of the same marriage.

Find baptisms of Doyle children with John and Bridget as parents. Pennsylvania Births and Christenings (1709-1950) is name-searchable. A baptism naming both parents places each child with the couple, which the census alone may not show. Search by father John Doyle and mother Bridget, then by surname Doyle at each Schuylkill parish, because Irish Catholic baptisms often name the mother by first name only.

Find parish register entries that name both Doyle and Halloran when the indexed baptism search misses them. Run a full-text co-occurrence search with Doyle and Halloran as separate terms, unscoped to a single collection, because Catholic sacramental registers are held at the parish or diocese (Diocese of Philadelphia for Schuylkill) and are not indexed by name for many years. Priests may spell Halloran as Holleran or Halloran, so run the variant too.

Find burials of John Doyle and of any child who died young. Seven of Bridget's nine children did not survive to 1900 (log_002), and their deaths are likely in parish burial registers or cemetery records. Pennsylvania Cemetery Records (ca. 1700-1950) and Pennsylvania Deaths and Burials (1720-1999) are both name-searchable. Pennsylvania has no statewide civil death registration before 1906, so these are the main route. Search each child's burial by surname Doyle.

Check the United States Mortality Schedules (1850-1880), which are name-searchable, for deaths in the Doyle household in the census years. A death of a child or of John Doyle in a census year is recorded here with the age and cause, and the schedule can give a child's name when no burial record survives.

Find John Doyle's estate file, held by the Schuylkill County Register of Wills, which lists heirs by name. The collection Pennsylvania, Probate Records (1683-1994) is browse-only, so this is an image browse of the county's dockets, not a name search. The date range runs from John's plausible death to Bridget's probable death, since a probate filed for either may name the children. Probate filed by Bridget herself after John died is also in scope.

Find Bridget's own death and burial record, under the surnames Doyle and Kearney. Her death record and obituary usually list surviving children by name, which can identify the children the 1900 census left out. Pennsylvania Deaths and Burials (1720-1999) is name-searchable, and Pennsylvania Cemetery Records (ca. 1700-1950) can supply the burial. Search Bridget under both surnames and the Halloran maiden name.

Associates test (FAN): search for Bridget's Halloran siblings and in-laws in Schuylkill households in 1860, 1870 and 1880. A sibling's household can name Bridget as Mrs. Doyle or give a niece or nephew name matching a Doyle child, and a sibling's record may name the children of John and Bridget. Search the surname Halloran with Irish birthplaces and neighbours who share the Doyle household's census page.

## Muhlenberg County, Kentucky — c. 1870-1890

Statewide death certificates begin 1911; no certificate can cover a death in the 1870s-1880s. County death registers (1804888) exist but the 1860s-1870s coverage is partial. For this era, **probate records are the primary death evidence**: administrator bonds name the widow or heir, estate settlements are dated, and register entries bracket the death within months. Muhlenberg County probate (1875188) survives well for the 1870s and is browse-only. Supplement with church burials, cemetery records, and census bracketing.

The statewide death certificates in Kentucky Deaths, 1911-1967 (collection 1417491) are the only certificates the question names. A certificate exists only if Elijah lived past 1911, which would make him about 97 years old. Searching it tests that possibility and rules it in or out. Name-searchable.

The locality entry names probate as the primary death evidence for a death before 1911. Administrator bonds name the widow or adult son, and estate settlements are dated, so together they bracket the death within months and place it in the county. Kentucky Probate Records, 1727-1990 (collection 1875188) is browse-only, organized by county and volume, so this is an image browse of Muhlenberg County volumes rather than a name search. The range runs to the collection's last year because an estate file can be assembled years after a death.

The locality entry names church burial registers and cemetery records as a way to bracket the death. A burial entry or headstone gives a date and place of death, and it can also say which church or cemetery he was buried in. Pursue this where the probate browse does not settle the date. The locality entry gives no collection ids for these records, so the repository is left general.

The locality entry names tax lists as a way to set the last-known-alive date. A tax list showing him in a year and his absence the next helps bracket the death window alongside the 1880 census and the probate browse. Shares the county's probate collection structure, so it is browsed, not name-searched.

Friends-and-neighbors item for an undated-event question. Settlements of neighbors' estates in Kentucky Probate Records (collection 1875188, browse-only) can name Elijah as a bondsman, appraiser, creditor or purchaser, which would place him in the county and bracket his last appearance. Such records often name the people closest to a death, so this can point to the estate file in item 5 or a family member who can confirm the death.

## Lincolnshire, England - 1750-1800

FamilySearch's 'England, Births and Christenings' collection (1473014) is a partial Legacy index: it does not index all records for this place or period, and no records or corrections are being added — a nil there is a statement about the index, not proof that no christening exists; search the parish register itself before concluding absence. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/England,_Births_and_Christenings_-_FamilySearch_Historical_Records)

planItems.rationale: Mary Dawson's own baptism (tree birth fact: about 1772, Lincolnshire). A baptism names her father and often her mother, so it is the most direct route to the parents. The locality entry loc_001 lists the England, Births and Christenings collection (1473014) as name-searchable, but it is a partial Legacy index, so a nil result proves nothing; search the parish register itself before concluding absence. Her parish is not yet known, so search the whole county by name and date.

Marriage of the candidate parents, to be identified once the father's name is known. It confirms the couple as a unit, dates their union against Mary's birth, and where this was the mother's first marriage it gives her maiden name. Because a remarriage is possible, also search for any earlier marriage of the mother. The marriage alone does not prove Mary is their child; that needs a record placing her with them. Collection 1473014, name-searchable, with the same partial-index caveat as item 1.

FAN search: baptisms of Mary's siblings, and of children sponsored by the same godparents, in the same parish. A sibling's baptism naming the same parents places Mary in that household without relying on her own entry. Godparents are the associates to test; a shared surname with a witness is a lead, not proof. Collection 1473014, name-searchable, with the partial-index caveat.

Mary's own marriage (she would be about 18 to 43). Marriage entries often name the bride's father, or give her parish, which can identify the parents. Search under Dawson and any variant spelling. Collection 1473014, name-searchable, with the partial-index caveat.

Mary's burial or death entry, dated after her last known life. The tree holds no death or burial fact for her. Burial entries sometimes state age or parish, which can point back to a baptism when the birth register has a gap. Collection 1473014, name-searchable, with the partial-index caveat.

Probate of a candidate father, dated to his lifespan: a father of a child born about 1772 could have died anywhere from about 1772 to about 1832, so the window is set by that lifespan and not by Mary's. A will or administration naming a daughter Mary would be direct evidence of parentage. The locality entry has no name-searchable probate collection for this place, so plan it as an archive or image search: the catalog check returned no collection in this session.

Fallback for item 1: if the name-indexed baptism search finds nothing, browse the parish register images for the years around Mary's birth. The partial Legacy index can miss an entry that the register holds. The catalog check returned no image group in this session, so the exact register must be confirmed before browsing.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

items.guide_markdown:
## Württemberg, Germany - 1780-1830

German children baptised with two or more given names were often called by the second in daily life (the wiki's example: Johann Christoph and Johann Friedrich were usually called Christoph and Friedrich) — search later records under the second given name alone as well as the full baptismal name. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Germany_Naming_Customs)

planItems.rationale: Subject I1 (Anna Margaretha Bauer) has one tree fact, a Birth dated 1792 in Württemberg, with no source and no FamilySearch ID, so no hints review applies. A baptism in the parish register names the father and mother directly, which is the core parentage evidence. Germany Births and Baptisms, 1558-1898 (collection 1473000, name-searchable per the locality entry loc_001) covers the birth window. Per the locality quirk, search under Anna Margaretha and also under Margaretha alone, because the second given name was often used in daily life.

Dedicated parents'-marriage item. Germany Marriages, 1558-1929 (collection 1473009, name-searchable per loc_001) is searched on the surname Bauer for couples marrying before the subject's birth. The marriage confirms the couple as a unit and, if it was the mother's first marriage, gives her maiden name. It does not by itself show that Anna is their child; that needs the baptism or a record placing her with them. No remarriage is suspected yet, so no earlier-marriage companion item is added.

FAN item. Search the same birth register (collection 1473000) for other Bauer baptisms in the years around 1792 and for the godparents named at them. Sibling baptisms name the same parents, and godparents are usually kin or neighbours who can point to the family. The parish is not yet known, so the search runs across Württemberg first and is narrowed once pli_001 names the parish.

Subject's own marriage. Germany Marriages, 1558-1929 (collection 1473009, name-searchable) may name her father, and her marriage is the one later record of her life that can state a parent's name. Search under Anna Margaretha Bauer and under Margaretha Bauer, since the second given name may have been used.

Fallback for pli_001. If the name index does not return the baptism, browse the images of the parish birth register for 1792 page by page. No volume was returned by volume_search for this place, so the register must be identified from the parish named in the baptism or from the FamilySearch Catalog once the parish is known.

## Locality Guide: Trysil, Hedmark, Norway (1780–1880)

### Jurisdictional Context

Trysil became its own *prestegjeld* in 1780, separated from Elverum. The 1860 death falls squarely within Trysil's own records. Administratively: Amt of Hedmark from 1781; Sorenskriveri of Søndre Østerdalen; Diocese of Oslo/Christiania 1537–1864, then Hamar.

### Church Records — Primary Source

- **Digitized images** (browse-only, 0% name-indexed): Kirkebøker 1588–1928 (Trysil prestegjeld) at FamilySearch Catalog (cat. 737) and Digitalarkivet. The 1860 burial will be in volume 008679203_003 (1814–1877, 325 images).
- **Indexed national extracts** (name-searchable): Norway Burials 1666–1927 (FS col 1468081; also Ancestry, MyHeritage); Norway Baptisms 1634–1927 (FS col 1467014); Norway Marriages 1660–1926 (FS col 1468080).
- **Dissenter church**: Trysil Frimenighet 1858–1920 at Digitalarkivet (images).

### Census

| Year | FS Collection | Access | Notes |
|------|--------------|--------|-------|
| 1801 | 3733603 | indexed & images | Subject ~21; also Ancestry, MyHeritage |
| 1865 | 3756102 | indexed & images | Postdates death; shows widow/children |
| 1870 | 4135961 | indexed & images | Postdates death |
| 1875 | 1529106 | indexed & images | Postdates death; also Ancestry, MyHeritage |

### Probate

- Norway Probate Index Cards 1640–1903 (FS col 1661306): indexed — locate the 1860 estate filing here.
- Skifteprotokoller image volumes at FS Catalog cover through 1853; post-1853 volumes held at Riksarkivet/Digitalarkivet.

### Land Records

- Pantebøker (mortgage/property) 1712–1860 (FS Catalog 489152) — images.

### Military / Levy Rolls

Norway's conscription/levy rolls (*lægdsruller*) began 1789. Each enrolled boy is listed under his father's name — direct parentage evidence. A male born ~1780 would appear from approximately 1789. Access via Riksarkivet and Digitalarkivet.

### Farm Books (*Bygdebøker*)

Trysilboka (Lillevold, Larsen, Bryn; FS Library 948.23/T2 D2l) — multiple volumes covering farm histories and resident genealogies for Trysil with personal name indexes in volumes 1–3, 7–8. High-value source for locating a household at the farm level.

### Key Access Points

- **FamilySearch** (free): indexed burials/baptisms/marriages/census, browse church record images
- **Digitalarkivet** (free): church books at media.digitalarkivet.no/en/kb/browse
- **Ancestry** (subscription): Norway Burials/Baptisms/Marriages extracts, 1865 census
- **MyHeritage** (subscription): Norway Burials/Marriages, 1865/1875 census
- **FamilySearch Library** (on-site or center): Trysilboka farm book, catalog microfilm

## Kongsberg Parish, Buskerud, Norway — Locality Guide (1760–1810)

**Ecclesiastical jurisdiction:** Kongsberg prestegjeld, Kongsberg prosti, Oslo bispedømme (until 1948). Civil jurisdiction in 1780: Buskerud amt (from 1680), Numedal og Sandsvær sorenskriveri, Kongsberg Byfogderi (probate/skifterett).

### Church Records

All Kongsberg church record volumes at FamilySearch are **browse-only** (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable). Browse image by image.

**Key FamilySearch volumes for a ~1780 baptism:**
- **008680156_003** (1769–1782, 382 images) — prime target for a ~1780 birth
- **008680157_002** (1783–1797, 249 images) — wider date window fallback
- **008680157_003** (1795–1816, 380 images)
- **009061212** (Kongsberg + Jondalen combined, 1696–1915, 691 images)

**National indexed extracts (searchable):**
- Norway Baptisms 1634–1927 (FS col 1467014): 28,370 Kongsberg records — search first; coverage of 1780s may be incomplete
- Norway Marriages 1660–1926 (FS col 1468080)
- Norway Burials 1666–1927 (FS col 1468081)
- Same extracts also at Ancestry (Norway Select Baptisms col 60092) and MyHeritage

**Digitalarkivet:** Complete parish register scans 1696–1969 at media.digitalarkivet.no (Buskerud county, Kongsberg prestegjeld). Both Kongsberg proper and Jondalen sub-parish registers are available. Same material as FS volumes; browse by year range.

### Census Records
- 1801 census (FS col 3733603, indexed + images; also Digitalarkivet, Ancestry, MyHeritage)
- No pre-1801 national census; the mine rolls below partially fill this gap

### Kongsberg Sølvverk (Silver Mine) Records
Special census-type rolls at Digitalarkivet for mine employees:
- Pensjonister (pensioners) 1711; Borgere (citizens/residents) 1723; Funksjonærer (officials) 1765
These predate the ~1780 birth but may document a father employed at the mine.

### Military / Conscription (Lægdsruller)
Norwegian levy rolls began 1789. A male born ~1780 enrolled ~age 7–9, listed directly **under his father's name** — direct parentage evidence. Access: Digitalarkivet (browse and search) and Riksarkivet physical holdings for Numedal og Sandsvær lægd.

### Probate Records
- Kongsberg Byfogderi Skifteprotokoller 1739–1851 (FS Catalog 437559, browse-only; also Digitalarkivet)
- Norway Probate Index Cards 1640–1903 (FS col 1661306, indexed)
- Kongsberg deanery probate 1741–1816 at Digitalarkivet

### Land and Property
- Pantebøker (mortgage books) 1721–1864 at FamilySearch Catalog (no. 485469, Kongsberg Byfogderi)

quirks: Although Mexicans use two surnames, most indexed records carry only the first (paternal) surname — search with the paternal surname alone; when the person is not found, search through the parents (a parent search with each parent's first surname, leaving out the child's name). ## Hamre prestegjeld, Hordaland, Norway - 1765-1800

Norwegian name spellings were set by the recorder and vary between records (the wiki's example: the given name Sivert written as Syver, Sjur, Siver, Sifuer or Siffuer) — search given-name spelling variants, not just the tree's spelling, before concluding a nil. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Norway_Church_Records)

planItems.rationale: Primary target: the marriage of a bride named Unna Halsteinsdatter (born May 1745 at Hestdal, Meland). The loc_001 entry lists Norway, Marriages, 1660-1926 (collection 1468080) as name-searchable, and Meland's marriages are in the Hamre kirkebøker. Search the bride under spelling variants (Unna, Unne, Unni, Una; Halsteinsdatter, Halstensdatter, abbreviated Halsteinsd./dtr.), per the loc_001 quirk on recorder spellings. Also search by place and date without a surname, since the groom is unknown. Patronymic per the Norway Naming Customs page: Halsteinsdatter means daughter of Halstein. The marriage date window is 1765-1800: she was 20 in 1765, and the entry's time period runs to 1800.

Dependency and parentage: the baptism of Unna born May 1745 at Hestdal. The tree holds only her birth fact and no baptism or parents. Norway Baptisms, 1634-1927 (collection 1467014) is name-searchable per loc_001. The entry names her father as Halstein, so the baptism confirms the patronymic and names the parents. It also gives the family whose members (FAN item below) may appear in marriage entries. Search name variants as in item 1.

Fallback to item 1 if the indexed marriage search for the bride returns nothing: browse the page images of the Hamre kirkebøker marriage volumes for the window, reading entries for Hestdal and Meland. The index may omit or misspell the bride. The volume search for this place returned no image groups in this session, so the volume must be located through the FamilySearch catalog or the localities entry before browsing. Marked as a fallback since the first indexed search may already settle the question.

FAN, required on an event question with an unknown spouse: marriages in the same parish of Hestdal siblings or cousins whose father is Halstein. A sibling's marriage entry names the same parents, and may name Unna as a witness or relative, or give the groom's home farm. Norway Marriages, 1660-1926 (collection 1468080) is name-searchable per loc_001. Search the father's given name Halstein with spelling variants, as the loc_001 quirk advises.

The subject's own burial or death entry, to be read for a 'wife of' or 'widow of' note that names the husband, and for the date she was last known alive. No death date is in the tree. Her lifespan from birth in 1745 bounds the window, so it runs to about 1835, not to the marriage. Burial registers in the Hamre kirkebøker are covered by the loc_001 parish record. Search name variants as in item 1.

If Unna married before 1801, the 1801 census household would show her with a husband and children. The locality entry lists no census collection, and this session's collection search for Norway returned nothing, so the availability of the 1801 census must be confirmed before searching. Searching it is conditional: if item 1 and item 3 find the marriage, this item corroborates the household; if they do not, it tests whether she was still unmarried in 1801.

Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.
